title: Environmental accounting

definition.text: A branch of accounting that measures, analyses and reports money and non-money information about environmental impacts.

facts.text: For a company it judges environmental performance and informs people inside and outside the firm; for a nation or region it records how the economy affects the environment.
It tracks resource use and environmental costs such as clean-up of contaminated sites, fines and taxes, pollution-prevention technology and waste handling.

A system combines environmentally differentiated accounting, which measures nature's effects on the firm in money, and ecological accounting, which measures the firm's effects on nature in physical units.
The field is divided into global, national and corporate environmental accounting.
At national level it is formalised internationally through SEEA, which builds on the System of National Accounts.
A 2007 United Nations assessment found environmental-economic accounting in use in 49 countries.
Explanations for why organisations do it range from manager and shareholder interests to legitimacy, stakeholder pressure and normative accountability.

title: Environmental management accounting

definition.text: The branch of corporate environmental accounting that supports a firm's internal decisions with physical and money data on its environmental use and costs.

facts.text: It gathers physical data on energy, water, materials and waste plus money data on environment-related costs, earnings and savings.
Corporate environmental accounting splits into this internal branch and environmental financial accounting, which reports to investors, lenders and other outsiders.

title: Environmental reporting

definition.text: The disclosure of an organisation's environmental impacts and performance.

facts.text: It may cover environmental risks and liabilities, energy and waste costs, emissions and pollution controls.
It reaches stakeholders through annual reports, sustainability reports, integrated reports and websites.

title: Environmental full-cost accounting

definition.text: A cost-accounting method that gathers the possible environmental costs and benefits of each option under consideration, tracing direct costs and allocating indirect ones.

facts.text: It is one part of true cost accounting, alongside human and social capital.
Experts find both 'full' and 'true' troublesome labels because the words are subjective.
It counts costs as resources are used, not when cash is spent: a vehicle bought once is costed over its working life, for example ten years.
It values goods even when no cash changes hands, such as equipment paid for by a state grant.
It includes overheads, and past costs such as buying equipment and future ones such as closing a facility.
Subsidies to energy and food keep prices artificially low, hiding true costs and the externalities of fossil fuels and mechanised farming.
Florida uses it to identify and report the actual costs of solid waste management.
A major motive is anticipating market or regulatory problems that come from ignoring the whole outcome of a process.

title: True cost accounting in food and farming

definition.text: The use of full or true cost accounting to price the hidden environmental and social costs of food production and waste.

facts.text: The FAO's 2014 and 2015 studies applied it to food wastage and to world food production's impact on natural capital.
The FAO put food wastage's yearly hidden cost at US$700 billion to natural capital and US$900 billion to social capital.
It estimated the environmental damage of world food production at US$2330 billion per year.

title: Green accounting

definition.text: Accounting that tries to bring environmental costs into the financial results of an activity.

facts.text: Its backers argue that GDP ignores the environment, so policymakers need a model that includes green accounting.
Its main aim is to help businesses manage trade-offs between ordinary economic goals and environmental goals.
It is said to secure only weak sustainability, a step toward strong sustainability.
Critics say depletion may already be counted in extraction industries and that valuing externalities can be arbitrary.
Economist Peter Wood brought the term into common use in the 1980s.
Environmental or green national accounting values environmental assets that national wealth measures usually leave out, partly because they are hard to value.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether green accounting is sound, since depletion may already be counted and externality values may be arbitrary.

title: Environmentally adjusted net domestic product

definition.text: A 'green' version of net domestic product that subtracts the using up of natural assets, also called EDP or Green NDP.

facts.text: The System of National Accounts defines net domestic product as net exports plus final consumption plus net investment.
Green accounting instead follows SEEA, which measures the depletion of scarce natural resources and the cost of environmental degradation and its prevention.
EDP adds net accumulation of produced and non-produced economic assets but deducts the net accumulation of non-produced natural assets.

title: Natural capital accounting

definition.text: The process of calculating the total stocks and flows of natural resources and services in an ecosystem or region.

facts.text: The accounts can be kept in physical units or in money, and can guide government, business and consumer choices about using resources and land.
Approaches include broad indicator dashboards, composite indices, overconsumption indices such as adjusted net savings and ecological footprints, and adjusted economic indicators such as green GDP.
Money-based indicators tend to be expressed as flows and physical indicators as stocks.
International support began with the 1987 Brundtland Report and the 1992 Rio Summit, whose Agenda 21 asked signatories to develop quantitative information on their activities.
The 2012 Rio+20 conference was described as a watershed in worldwide interest in the field.
The Netherlands, France and the Philippines were early adopters of integrated environmental-economic accounts.
A US study estimated that air-pollution damages from coal-fired power generation range from 0.8 to 5.6 times the value the industry adds.
The US Congress halted federal work on environmental accounting in 1994, after the first US integrated satellite accounts appeared.

title: Wealth Accounting and Valuation of Ecosystem Services
article: Natural capital accounting#Wealth Accounting and Valuation of Ecosystem Services Partnership

definition.text: WAVES is a World Bank-led global partnership that helps countries put the value of natural capital into their national accounts.

facts.text: It was launched in October 2010 at the Convention on Biological Diversity's COP-10 meeting in Japan.
Its projects in countries such as Botswana, Colombia and Madagascar built capacity to apply SEEA.
The World Bank now runs a successor, the Global Program for Sustainability.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
chapter: National and corporate natural capital accounts

title: Repetto's green accounts for Indonesia

definition.text: A 1990 World Resources Institute study that adjusted Indonesia's national accounts for the depletion of its natural resources.

facts.text: It subtracted the net depreciation of petroleum, timber and soils from GDP to estimate an environmentally adjusted net domestic product.
It found conventional accounts overstated net income and its growth.
Environmental costs equalled 4.9% of Indonesia's NDP in 1990, mainly from land-use change and oil extraction.

notes: Country case, kept because it is a pioneering study of green national accounting; drop if selection prefers no country cases.

title: Sustainability accounting

definition.text: Accounting, also called social and environmental accounting or non-financial reporting, that discloses information about a firm's social and environmental performance to outsiders such as investors and creditors.

facts.text: It began in the 1970s and is treated as a branch of financial accounting.
In management accounting it supports internal decisions about the firm's economic, ecological and social performance, the triple bottom line of people, planet and profit.
Corporate sustainability reporting and triple bottom line accounting are its best-known measures.
The Global Reporting Initiative was set up to give organisations guidelines so that social and environmental reports are consistent.
In the 1970s environmental matters were part of a broad social accounting movement; by 1991–1995 environmental accounting almost completely dominated social accounting.
In most countries governments do not require companies to prepare and publish sustainability reports.
The Sustainability Accounting Standards Board standardises some sustainability metrics so investors can judge corporate risk.

title: SEEA Ecosystem Accounting
article: System of Integrated Environmental and Economic Accounting#Ecosystem accounts

definition.text: SEEA EA is a statistical framework that gives a consistent accounting approach for measuring ecosystems.

facts.text: Its accounts present the extent and condition of ecosystems and the services they provide, in physical and money terms and tied to location.
The UN Statistical Commission adopted it as a standard at its 52nd session in March 2021.
An AI-powered tool, the ARIES for SEEA Explorer, was released in April 2021 for rapid, standardised natural capital accounting.
Its forerunner, the SEEA Experimental Ecosystem Accounts, built ecosystem accounts even though many of the stocks and flows are non-market assets.

title: Residence principle in emission accounts
article: System of Integrated Environmental and Economic Accounting#Flows of materials and energy

definition.text: The SEEA rule that counts all emissions caused by a country's economy, wherever they happen, rather than those released inside its borders.

facts.text: UNFCCC climate inventories use geographic borders, so the two approaches differ mainly for transport.
Under SEEA, emissions from trucks, ships or aircraft go to their home country even when released abroad.
UNFCCC inventories treat transport as its own sector, hiding the shares of households and industries.

title: True cost accounting

definition.text: An accounting approach that measures and puts values on the hidden effects of economic activity on the environment, society and health.

facts.text: It is also called full cost accounting or multiple capital accounting, and covers natural, human, social and produced capital.
The hidden effects are costs and benefits not reflected in market prices or in firms' profit and loss accounts.
It is closely tied to externalities and traces back to the work of Pigou and Marshall in the 1920s.
It is seen as an extension of cost-benefit analysis that adds systems thinking about many stakeholders and capitals.
A typical study uses a dozen or more indicators across environmental, health, social and economic domains.
Much of its development has been in food and farming, where hidden costs can be large.
Greenhouse gas emissions are easy to include, but effects on working conditions or cultural identity are harder to find.

title: Hidden costs of global agrifood systems
article: True cost accounting#Hidden costs of global agrifood systems

definition.text: Estimates of the environmental, health and social costs of the world's food systems that market prices leave out.

facts.text: FOLU (2019) put them at USD 12 trillion and Hendricks et al. (2023) at USD 19 trillion, with a range of USD 7.2 to 51.8 trillion.
The FAO's 2023 State of Food and Agriculture estimated USD 12.7 trillion, assessed country by country for 154 countries.
FAO later found health costs from unhealthy diets made up 70 percent of all agrifood hidden costs in 2020.

notes: The three global estimates use different methods and scopes, so they are stated as separate facts rather than conflicts.

title: Asset

definition.text: In financial accounting, any resource a business or other economic entity owns or controls.

facts.text: It is anything, physical or not, that can be used to produce economic value.
A firm's balance sheet records the money value of its assets.
Tangible assets include current assets such as cash and inventory and fixed assets such as land, buildings and equipment; intangible assets include patents and goodwill.
Ownership is not needed: an asset is recognised if the entity controls it, so a leased building counts but employees do not.
The balance sheet follows the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities plus equity.
Fixed assets except land are written off against profits over their expected life through depreciation.
In economics, an asset is any form in which wealth can be held, and social scientists study how things like ecosystems are turned into assets.

title: Wasting asset

definition.text: An asset that loses value irreversibly over time.

facts.text: Examples include vehicles, machinery and options contracts, and mines and quarries in use.
Its decline may be handled for tax and other purposes through depreciation.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Depletion (accounting)

definition.text: An accounting and tax method that records the gradual using up of natural resources such as minerals, oil and timber as an expense over time.

facts.text: Depletion means using up natural resources by mining, quarrying, drilling or felling.
Like depreciation, it lets owners recover costs as a resource's reserves shrink.
For tax there are two types, percentage depletion and cost depletion; standing timber must use cost depletion.
Cost depletion spreads the resource's total cost over the estimated quantity, charging a share for each unit extracted.
Example: if a well holding 200,000 barrels cost $100,000 and 10,000 barrels are extracted in year one, the deduction is $5,000.
Percentage depletion multiplies a set percentage for each mineral by the property's gross income for the year.
It uses country data to estimate the adjustments needed for the use and depletion of a nation's natural capital.
Environmentalists use it to track resource use over time and hold governments to account; economists use it to see how reliant countries or firms are on non-renewable resources.

title: Environmental profit and loss account

definition.text: A company's money valuation of its environmental impacts across its own operations and its supply chain, from raw materials to the factory gate.

facts.text: It internalises externalities by counting the ecosystem services a business depends on as well as the damage it causes.
Its main purpose is to show managers and stakeholders how large the impacts are and where in the supply chain they occur.
The first one was Puma's, on 2010 data, valuing greenhouse gases, water use, other air pollution, land conversion and waste.
Its method built on input-output models and valuation work in environmental economics such as the TEEB study.
Philips's 2017 annual report put its environmental impact for that year at Euro 7.2 billion using this method.
Preparing one can be expensive, and it is seen as a first step toward prices that reflect use of environmental goods and services.

title: Gross ecosystem product

definition.text: A statistic giving the money value of the ecosystem services produced in an area over an accounting period, usually a year.

facts.text: It supplements GDP, which counts only market values and so misses the non-market value of ecosystem services.
It sums material services such as fish, regulating services such as pollination and cultural services such as tourism, using market and non-market valuation.
Zhiyun Ouyang and Chunquan Zhu first proposed it in 2013.
A 2020 study of Qinghai province in China found nearly 80% of the benefits in its GEP flowed to other provinces.
The UN Statistical Commission adopted it within SEEA Ecosystem Accounting in 2021.
China issued official GEP accounting guidelines in October 2022 and uses it in rural development, payments for ecosystem services and urban planning.

title: Integrated reporting

definition.text: Corporate reporting that produces a periodic integrated report on how a firm's strategy, governance, performance and prospects create value over time.

facts.text: It presents financial and other value-relevant information together, aimed mainly at those who allocate financial capital.
Backers argue firms must preserve value from non-financial resources such as people, intellectual property and nature, not just investors' money.
It calls for adding ecological data, such as greenhouse gas emissions, alongside financial figures.
A 2009 meeting convened by the Prince of Wales set up the International Integrated Reporting Committee, renamed a Council in November 2011, to create a global framework.
From 2010 the Johannesburg Stock Exchange required listed companies to issue an integrated report or explain why not.
In 2021 the IIRC and SASB merged into the Value Reporting Foundation, which the IFRS Foundation folded into its International Sustainability Standards Board by June 2022.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Material flow accounting

definition.text: The measurement of material flows through a national or regional economy, also called economy-wide material flow analysis.

facts.text: It records materials entering an economy, changes in its stocks, and outputs as exports or as discharges to the environment.
It treats the economy as a subsystem inside the environment that, like a living thing, needs a constant throughput of materials and energy, an idea called industrial or societal metabolism.
It covers all solid, liquid and gaseous materials moved by people or livestock except bulk water and air, usually in tonnes per year.
Materials are grouped into biomass, fossil energy carriers, metals and non-metallic minerals.
It counts non-market flows such as grazed biomass and mining waste rock, which made up 21% of global extraction in 2010.
It is a satellite system to the national accounts and is used in SEEA.
It counts all materials humans mobilise except bulk water and air, usually in tonnes per year.
Direct material input is domestic extraction plus imports; domestic material consumption is domestic extraction plus imports minus exports.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature
chapter: National and corporate natural capital accounts

title: Material flow indicators

definition.text: Standard indicators calculated from material flow accounts to summarise an economy's material use.

facts.text: Direct material input is domestic extraction plus imports; domestic material consumption is domestic extraction plus imports minus exports.
The physical trade balance is imports minus exports, the reverse of the money trade balance because goods and money flow in opposite directions.
Total material requirement adds hidden flows, materials moved but not used such as mining overburden.
Raw material consumption counts raw materials embodied in traded goods, usually via environmentally extended input-output analysis.

title: SEEA-Water
article: System of Environmental and Economic Accounting for Water

definition.text: The UN's framework for organising physical and economic information about water with the same concepts and classifications as the System of National Accounts.

facts.text: The UN Statistical Commission adopted it as an interim statistical standard in 2007.
It organises water stocks and flows into the inland water resources system, covering the natural water cycle, and the economy, covering water-using industries and households.
Its SNA compatibility lets hydrological and water-use data be combined with economic data.
More than fifty countries are implementing or planning water accounts.

title: Triple bottom line

definition.text: An accounting framework that judges an organisation on three results: social, environmental and economic.

facts.text: In ordinary accounting the 'bottom line' is profit or loss; the triple bottom line adds social and environmental bottom lines.
Freer Spreckley first set out the framework in 1981, and John Elkington says he coined the phrase in 1994 and developed it in his 1997 book Cannibals with Forks.
Elkington's slogan 'people, planet, and profit' later titled Shell's first sustainability report in 1997.
The planet line asks firms to cut their ecological footprint, and often to use life cycle assessment to find a product's true environmental cost.
The profit line means economic value created after deducting all input costs including capital, which differs from accounting profit.
Measuring the people line is relatively new, problematic and often subjective.
Since a 2007 UN and ICLEI standard it has been the dominant approach to public-sector full cost accounting.
Critics say it treats the environment as a background externality and is hard to apply in practice.

contested_note: Many people disagree that the triple bottom line is the right way to improve social and environmental conditions, citing reductive treatment of the environment and weak practical application.

title: El Serafy depletion cost method

definition.text: Salah El Serafy's method for valuing the depletion cost of natural resources, one of several alternatives for estimating resource rent in national accounts.

facts.text: Other methods compared with it are net price, sustainable price, transaction value and replacement cost.
El Serafy co-edited 'Economic Accounting for Sustainable Development', a report from UNEP-World Bank workshops held after 1983.
He disagreed with Anne Harrison: she wanted adjustments inside the existing SNA, while he proposed redefining intermediate and final demand.

contested_note: Harrison and El Serafy disagreed on whether to adjust indicators within the existing national accounts or to redefine intermediate and final demand.
notes: Sources name the method but do not describe how its user cost is calculated; consider a gap-fill crawl.

title: Net domestic product

definition.text: Net domestic product (NDP) is gross domestic product minus the depreciation of a country's capital goods.

facts.text: NDP accounts for capital consumed during the year, such as the wearing out of housing, vehicles and machinery.
The depreciation deducted is often called the capital consumption allowance, the amount needed to replace the depreciated assets.
Investment that only replaces worn-out equipment keeps output up but adds nothing to the economy's capacity, so rising GDP from higher replacement spending would not make anyone better off.
Some economists therefore see NDP as a better measure of social and economic well-being than GDP.
A growing gap between GDP and NDP signals increasing obsolescence of capital goods; a narrowing gap means the capital stock is improving.
NDP adjusted for resource depletion, called EDP, was proposed as a green alternative but was not formally included in the System of National Accounts.
